global.headline: US sends third carrier to Gulf as Trump floats post-midterm bombing
summary: The Wall Street Journal reported Washington is sending a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, with Marine Corps ships and up to 10,000 more troops, arriving by late November. Two carriers are already on station.Trump told TIME that renewed large-scale bombing after the November midterms was “possible” and that “by annihilating Iran, we've created peace in the world”, rejecting Tehran's seven-day Hormuz offer as insufficient. He separately vowed to hit Iran “very hard” if it is linked to the Flydubai cockpit attack.

UK counter-terrorism police arrested a 27-year-old dual British-Iranian in London over the RAF Fairford incident. Crude through Hormuz reached a seven-day average of 13.5m barrels a day, matching the pre-war baseline.
global.geopolitical: A carrier arriving in late November tells Tehran the war resumes after the midterms unless it concedes first. That removes any reason to settle now and gives the IRGC eight weeks to prepare rather than disarm.
global.socioeconomic: Shipping had begun pricing the strait as survivable, with barrels moving by pipeline, ship-to-ship transfer and naval escort. A third carrier re-prices the Gulf as a theatre again, lifting war-risk and freight premiums on cargo that is physically getting out.

global.headline: China halts fuel exports as Trump presses Europe to open reserves
summary: Reuters reported Chinese refiners have suspended exports of oil products beyond Hong Kong and Macau until further notice, with PetroChina cancelling October petrol and jet-fuel cargoes — removing a major supplier from an already short refined-products market.

Washington told Germany and France to release 120 million barrels of emergency diesel over six months or face a US export ban before the midterms. Britain, the European Commission, Germany, France, Italy and Ireland held a call on Thursday on drawing down reserves. The American Petroleum Institute warned a ban would raise costs at home.
Brent settled at US$102.31 (+4.4%) and WTI at US$92.87 (+2.7%), reversing an early fall. US retail diesel is about S$2.20 a litre (US$6.51 a gallon, 21 September).
global.geopolitical: Washington is rationing fuel to allies as leverage while Beijing withholds it as policy. Product exports have become an instrument of statecraft, which makes refining capacity — not crude reserves — the asset that now confers power.
global.socioeconomic: Diesel moves freight, farming and construction, and the shortage is not expected to ease before next year. Each week of it compounds into the cost base under food and goods prices in importing economies, Singapore among them.

global.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2002
summary: The 10-year US Treasury yield rose as high as 5.342% on Thursday, past its 2007 peak and the highest since early 2002, as a bond selloff accelerated. The 30-year is also at a 2002 high, and the global benchmark posted its biggest quarterly rise this century in the third quarter.

Traders cite persistent inflation, heavy federal borrowing and resilient growth, plus expectations that the Federal Reserve must tighten further while oil prices and the unresolved Middle East war keep feeding costs through.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage reached 7.28%, against 6.34% a year ago, pushing buyers towards adjustable-rate loans. Fed governor Lisa Cook named AI-driven inflation a leading risk for 2027.
global.geopolitical: The world's reference risk-free rate has repriced upward, so every government refinancing debt pays more. That tightens the fiscal room of states simultaneously funding wars, rearmament and energy subsidies.
global.socioeconomic: A 7.28% mortgage prices out a cohort of first-time buyers and locks existing owners into homes they cannot afford to move from. Higher US yields also pull capital from emerging markets and raise refinancing costs for corporate borrowers worldwide.

global.headline: Putin names Kaliningrad a nuclear red line as war budget rises 27%
summary: At the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Putin said Russia would use “all weapons in its arsenal”, nuclear included, if Kaliningrad were attacked — citing Baltic naval drills and attempts to detain Russian vessels. He said he had no plans to attack any European country.

He conceded Ukrainian strikes have cost Russia about 1% of GDP and destroyed more than 100 Russian vessels in the Black Sea. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Samara overnight, defying Trump, who blames the refinery campaign for high fuel prices.
The 2027 draft budget sets a record 17.1 trillion roubles for the military, up 27%, while cutting social policy 7%, education 6% and healthcare 6.8%. The 2026 deficit forecast has doubled to 3.2%.
global.geopolitical: Declaring Kaliningrad a nuclear tripwire converts a Baltic policing dispute into a stated red line. It lowers the threshold at which boarding a sanctioned tanker becomes an alliance-wide crisis.
global.socioeconomic: Russia is now financing the war from pensions, schools and hospitals. That is fiscally workable and politically corrosive: the cost of continuing has been shifted off the state's books and onto households.

global.headline: French school protests spread nationwide with 1,949 arrests in a day
summary: Police made 1,949 arrests and reported 305 officers injured on Thursday as secondary-school students set fires, blockaded entrances and clashed with police across France. A security source counted about 900 blockades and related incidents; protests reached more than 1,000 schools, over 160 closed, and public transport was suspended in several cities.

The grievances are overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long timetables and crumbling, overheated buildings. University students joined in Paris and Marseille, and several principals were injured or assaulted during blockades.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting; the government blamed the far left for the violence.
global.geopolitical: A French government absorbed by domestic unrest is a weaker party in this week's diesel-reserve bargaining and in European decisions on Ukraine, precisely when both require Paris to commit resources.
global.socioeconomic: The demands are for capacity the state has not funded — teachers, classrooms, maintenance. Meeting them costs money France lacks under its deficit path, so the government must either spend it or carry the disruption.

singapore.headline: Singapore launches first of four new offshore patrol vessels
summary: Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing officiated the launch of the Republic of Singapore Navy's first new offshore patrol vessel, Sentinel, at Fassmer's shipyard in Berne, Germany, on 1 October. It is the first of four, with the remainder under construction and progressive delivery from 2028.
The ship is 94.85m long with a 15.2m beam, displaces 2,700 tonnes, exceeds 23 knots and has endurance beyond 4,000 nautical miles, on a baseline crew of about 40.

It can launch manned and unmanned craft and carry containerised mission systems, so a single hull can be reconfigured between maritime security tasks. The four will replace the existing Sentinel-class Maritime Security and Response Vessels.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is buying endurance and reach rather than more hulls — a navy sized for sustained presence across crowded Malacca and South China Sea approaches, where staying on station matters more than firepower per ship.
singapore.socioeconomic: A crew of 40 on a 2,700-tonne ship is the real design decision. Facing the same shrinking cohort as every Singapore employer, the navy is growing capability through automation rather than through sailors.

singapore.headline: SIA and Scoot extend Dubai and Jeddah cancellations into December
summary: Singapore Airlines cancelled SQ494 and SQ495 between Singapore and Dubai until 1 December, and Scoot cancelled TR796 and TR797 to Jeddah until 2 December — extending suspensions rolled over repeatedly since the Iran war began in February.
SIA cited the geopolitical situation in the Middle East. Affected customers may claim a full refund of the unused portion of their ticket.
Dubai is the world's busiest international airport and a principal transfer point between Singapore and Europe, Africa and the Gulf; Jeddah is the gateway for Haj and Umrah travel.
singapore.geopolitical: Nine months is no longer a disruption but a redrawn network. Singapore's own direct reach into the Gulf has lapsed, and the connecting traffic has settled onto carriers routing through other hubs.
singapore.socioeconomic: Gulf business travel, pilgrimage and belly-hold freight now move through third hubs at a premium. Transfer traffic lost for this long does not automatically return when the routes do.

singapore.headline: HDB resale prices fall a third quarter as private prices rise 1.4%
summary: HDB flash estimates released on 1 October put the third-quarter resale price index at 202.4, down 0.2% on the quarter, after falls of 0.1% in Q1 and 0.3% in Q2 — a cumulative 0.6% over nine months.

Volume rose rather than fell: 7,528 resale transactions against 7,157 in the same quarter last year, up 5.2%. The decline persisted even after the 15-month wait-out period for private owners buying resale flats was lifted.

URA's flash estimate for the same quarter had private home prices up 1.4%. Separately, a Canberra Drive executive condominium site drew 13 bids, with a record top offer from a Santarli-led joint venture.
singapore.geopolitical: A public housing market that cools while the private market rises is the clearest evidence that Singapore's two-tier property system is now driven by different buyers — one domestic and policy-bound, one open to capital looking for a safe currency.
singapore.socioeconomic: For the first time in years, waiting is not punished: resale buyers face a falling index with more flats to choose from. Sellers planning to upgrade now face a widening gap between what they get and what they must pay.

singapore.headline: Beverage container deposit scheme becomes mandatory from 1 October
summary: From 1 October only beverages in containers carrying the Deposit Mark may be sold in Singapore, ending the six-month transition that began on 1 April. All pre-packaged drinks in plastic or metal containers from 150ml to 3,000ml now carry a 10-cent deposit, refundable at Return Right reverse vending machines.
There are roughly 1,300 machines nationwide. The scheme had collected more than 33 million containers by mid-September, against 5.5 million in early August.
Users reported a smooth process on the first day of full operation, though some small retailers said they would keep non-compliant stock for their own consumption.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore joins the deposit-return systems already standard across Northern Europe. For a country importing almost all its packaging and exporting none of its waste, recovery rates are a sovereignty question, not an environmental gesture.
singapore.socioeconomic: The deposit is regressive by design and refundable in practice, so the cost falls on whoever does not bother to return. The collection curve — six-fold in six weeks — suggests most people do.

singapore.headline: Study finds most young Singaporeans want children but misjudge fertility
summary: A Thomson Medical and National University of Singapore study, led by Reuben Ng of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, surveyed adults aged 18 to 39 and found 84% want children, while only one in ten answered all basic fertility questions correctly.

Among childless respondents who said having children mattered to them, 43% got two or fewer of five fertility-literacy questions right. Four in five knew pregnancy becomes less likely with age, but only 29% knew the ovaries do not keep producing new eggs.
More than half believed they were well informed. Singapore's total fertility rate stands at 0.87.
singapore.geopolitical: Every advanced economy treats low fertility as a resource question, and most respond with money. This finding points at something cash transfers cannot buy: a population that intends to have children later than biology allows.
singapore.socioeconomic: If desire is not the constraint, baby bonuses are aimed at the wrong target. The implied policy is information and earlier access to fertility services — both far cheaper than the subsidies now in use.

word.definition: Interchangeable with another unit of the same kind; substitutable without loss.
word.etymology: Medieval Latin fungibilis, from the legal phrase fungi vice, “to serve in place of”.
word.example: Crude is fungible and found other routes, so Hormuz lost its leverage; refining capacity is not, which is why China's export halt moved prices instead.
